text:
Motions of The Earth › Motions of The Earth › Motions of The Earth — Revision note (part 2/3)

**Equinoxes:**
 • When the earth moves around its orbit, it reaches two points during a year, where the tilt of the earth's axis causes it to be straight relative to that of the sun. These days are called equinoxes. **• Spring equinoxes:**On 20-21st March, the rays are directly falling on the equator, causing the duration of day and night equal throughout the earth. It is spring in the northern hemisphere, so it is called spring equinoxes. **• Autumnal equinoxes:**On 22-23rd September, the rays are directly falling on the equator, causing the duration of day and night equal throughout the earth. It is autumn in the northern hemisphere, so it is called autumnal equinoxes. **• A year:
 -**There are 365 days and 6 hours in a year. The time taken by the earth to complete its one revolution around the sun is called one year. - A leap year consists of 366 days. In a leap year, the February month has 29 days instead of 28 days. **• Rituchakra:**In our country, we have summer, rainy, and winter seasons. We divide the year into six seasons, namely, Vasant, Grishma, Varsha, Sharad, Hemant, and Shishir. The cycle of these six seasons is called the 'rituchakra.'
 **• Phases of the moon:
 -**The moon revolves around the earth, and the earth revolves around the sun. - The sun, moon, and the earth are not always in a straight line. - The moon doesn't have its own light, and we can see the moon only because of the sun's light, which falls on it. - We see the whole side of the moon on a full moon night while on a new moon night, we cannot see any side of the moon. - From new moon to full moon, the moon changes its shape every day. - From full moon to new moon, it becomes smaller and smaller and after 14 to 15 days it is new moon again and this period is known as Waning.

text:
The Four Domains of The Earth › The Four Domains of The Earth › The Four Domains of The Earth — Revision note (part 1/4)

• **Domains of the Earth:**
 • There are four realms of the Earth, also known as the four spheres of the life that interact with each other, are the **Atmosphere, Biosphere, Lithosphere, and Hydrosphere.**
 • Atmosphere is a blanket of gases surrounding the Earth, which is held in place by the Earth's gravitational pull. The atmosphere extends up to approximately 1600 km above the Earth's surface. The air in the atmosphere consists of majorly Nitrogen (78.1%), oxygen (20.9%), and argon (0.9%). Traces of several other gases like carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide, nitrous oxide, hydrogen, helium, neon, ozone, and methane, etc. are also present in the air.

• **Importance of atmosphere:**
 • Life supporting gases such as oxygen, nitrogen, and carbon dioxide are present in the atmosphere.
 • The atmosphere prevents the harmful ultraviolet rays of the sun from reaching us.
 • The atmosphere traps solar radiation and keeps the Earth warm.

• **Various layers of the Earth’s atmosphere:**

1. Troposphere
 2. Stratosphere
 3. Mesosphere
 4. Thermosphere
 5. Exosphere

• **The troposphere** is the first layer stretching from ground to 8km-18km above the Earth's surface. This layer is the most important because the air we breathe is present in this layer. All weather changes, such as the formation of clouds, rainfall, etc. as well as human activities, takes place in this layer.

• **The stratosphere** lies above the troposphere extending up to a height of 50 km. The ozone layer present in this layer protects us from the harmful ultravoilet rays of the sun. Jet aircrafts are allowed to fly in the stratosphere because this layer is very stable.

• **Mesosphere** lies above the stratosphere, extending up to a height of 50-80km. It is the coldest part of the Earth’s atmosphere.

title: The Four Domains of The Earth
text:
The Four Domains of The Earth › The Four Domains of The Earth › The Four Domains of The Earth — Revision note (part 2/4)

• **The thermosphere** stretches from 80-500 km above the surface of the Earth. The temperature is extremely hot in the thermosphere and gets warmer as we go higher. Here the air becomes thinner. At the lower level, this layer contains electrically charged particles. This layer is also known as the ionosphere, as it transmits radiowaves back to the Earth. The space shuttle orbits in this layer.

• **The exosphere** is the topmost layer or the uppermost limit of the atmosphere. It extends from 500-10000km. It contains light gases like hydrogen and helium. The tempreature is extremely hot in this layer.

• **The biosphere** is the interlinking zone where land, water, and air come in contact with each other. Life exists only in the biosphere, thus making Earth a unique planet. The biosphere is that part of the Earth where all the living beings exist and where the Lithosphere, Hydrosphere, and Atmosphere co-exist. Earth has countless species of plants and animals living in the biosphere. The biosphere consists of different ecosystems having their own climate, plants, and animals. The physical environment(i.e., the air, water, and land) and the biological environment( all living beings) are both interdependent on each other.

• **The lithosphere** is the outer solid layer of the Earth, including the Earth's crust and outermost mantle. It is 100km deep from the Earth's surface. The outermost layer that is known as the Earth’s crust varies in thickness. The oceanic crust below the oceans is about 5-10 km. The continental crust is about 35 km under the continents and about 60 km under the mountain ranges. The Lithosphere includes several landforms such as plateaus, plains, mountains, valleys, and ocean floors.

title: Major Landforms
text:
Major Landforms › Major Landforms › Major Landforms — Revision note (part 1/4)

• **Landforms** - Landforms are the physical features on the earth's surface that form boundaries between the countries, states, provinces, etc.
 • Various types of landforms are Mountains, Plains, Valleys, Plateaus, Hills, etc.

**1. Mountain:** Mountain is a high area with a steep slope that has an elevation greater than 1,000 ft. Above the sea level. They have different heights and shapes. When many mountains join together, they form a chain, and this chain is called as Mountain range. Mt. Everest is the world's highest mountain, at the height of 29,029 ft. above the sea level.
 [Figure 1]

• **Importance of mountains:**
 a. They form a natural barrier against the hot and cold winds.
 b. Mountains are rich in mineral resources and are home to rich flora and fauna.
 c. The cooler climate in the mountains attracts the tourists.

**2.** **Plateau:**Plateau is a mountain with a flat top having steep slopes. They are also called as tableland because of their shape. The highest plateau is the Plateau of Tibet. The oldest plateau is the Deccan plateau.
 [Figure 2]

**• Importance of plateau:**
 a. Plateaus have rich black soil.
 b. Plateaus have waterfalls and have deep canyons. For e.g., Jog falls in Karnataka and Grand Canyon in the USA.
 c. The natural scenic beauty of the plateaus attracts the tourists.

**3. Plains:** Plains are vast stretches of flat grassy areas. The plains are divided into Coastal plains and interior plains. Plains cover 55% of the earth's land surface, and approximately 90% of the earth's population lives on plains.
 [Figure 3]

**• Importance of plains:**
 a. Provide fertile land for cultivation.
 b. Plains are thickly populated and provide employment opportunities.

A river has its origin or source in the snow melting region or springs. It flows down the mountain valleys and plains into larger water bodies like lakes, oceans, and seas. • During its course, a river goes through three different stages:
 a. The **upper course**: In this course, the river is in its youthful stage and flows rapidly. It erodes and cuts through the mountains and forms waterfalls, gorges and canyons.
 b. The **middle course**: In this course, the speed of the river slightly decreases as it flows through gentle slopes. Here, the tributaries join the river, and thus it becomes broad. A tributary is a small stream or a river that joins a big river. As the flow of the river decreases, it starts depositing silt on both sides, thus making the plains fertile. It forms meanders or horse-shoe like loops.
 c. The **lower course**: In the lower course, the flow of the river slows down. It branches out into many smaller streams known as distributaries before it enters the sea. It deposits sediments, thus forming deltas. A very famous delta in India is The Sunderbans formed by the river Ganga in its lower course.

**• Importance of rivers:**
 a. Rivers provide water which we use for various purposes like irrigation, washing, cleaning, etc.
 b. Water is also required in industries for various processes.

title: Maps our Guides
text:
Maps our Guides › Maps our Guides › Maps our Guides — Revision note (part 1/2)

• A map is a drawing representing the whole area or a part of an area on a flat surface.
 • A map represents a small part of the earth’s surface or the entire earth.
 • Maps show us various places like the continents, countries, states, districts, cities, or neighbourhoods.

**• Merits of maps:**
 1. Maps tell us the size and shape of the countries and distance between the places.
 2. A map may even show a smaller area with great details such as the exact location of the houses and streets in a city or a neighbourhood.
 3. Maps are easy to carry around.

**• Limitations of maps:**
 1. The earth is round in shape, and a round surface cannot be shown accurately on a flat paper.

**• Map scale:**Map scale is defined as the ratio of the distance between two places on a map and their actual distance on the ground between those two places.
 **• The map scale is of two types:**
 a. A large scale map which represents a small area in great details.
 b. A small scale map represents a large area in less detail.

**• Directions: There are four cardinal directions i.e, East, West, North, and South.
 • The sub-directions are North-East, North-West, South-East and South-West.**

**•**A compass is an instrument which shows directions. The magnetic needle in the compass always points to the North-South direction.

**• Types of maps:
 1. Physical maps:** Maps which shows physical features of the earth like the mountains, plateaus, oceans, rivers, and lakes are called physical maps.
 **2. Political maps:** Political maps show the international borders, location of states, districts, and cities. These maps use different colours to show different countries.
 3.**Thematic maps:** Thematic maps represent only certain features like distribution of minerals, forests, types of weather, etc.

title: Maps our Guides
text:
Maps our Guides › Maps our Guides › Maps our Guides — Revision note (part 2/2)

**• Signs and symbols:**We use symbols to represent the natural or man-made features on the earth, such as buildings, trails, roads, bridges, and rivers.
 • A symbol is a dot, line or a drawing that represents something. For example; black dots represent cities, circled stars represent capital cities, and different types of lines represent boundaries, roads, highways and rivers.
 • These symbols on a map are called as conventional symbols.

**• Colours:**Sometimes, colours are used as symbols to share information on a map. Different colours are used to represent different things on the map.

**• On a physical map, the colour scheme followed is:**
 1) Blue: Water bodies
 2) Green: Plain areas
 3) Brown: Mountains, Deserts
 4) Dark yellow or light brown: Plateaus

**•**A map usually consists of a key that provides the scale of the map and also explains about the various symbols used in the map.

title: Major Rivers of India
text:
Major Rivers of India › Major Rivers of India › Major Rivers of India — Revision note (part 1/1)

• A river is any large natural stream of water.
 • A river flows in a channel, towards the sea, ocean, lake, or into another river.
 • There are two types of rivers:
  a. **Perennial rivers:** Are those rivers that show a constant water flow throughout the year except under extreme conditions of drought.
  b. **Non-perennial rivers:** These are the rivers that have no water for at least part of the year. Such rivers are seasonal in nature.

• The **Krishna River** is 4th largest river in India. It is also called Krishnaveni. Length:1,300 km.

• The **Kaveri River** originates in Karnataka. The river basin includes Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Kerala, Puducherry.

• In East Central India, the **Mahanadi**is a major river and is very important for the state of Odisha.

• The **Narmada**, also called Rewa, flows through central India. Also known as the 'Lifeline of Madhya Pradesh.'

• The **Indus river** is the major south-flowing river in South Asia and is the main supplier of water resources to Punjab and Sindh plains.

• The **Ganges**, also known as Ganga - most sacred river to the Hindus. Trans-boundary river - flows through India and Bangladesh. Originates in the Western Himalayas. Length: 2,525 km long.

• The **Yamuna**, also known as Jumna - one of the largest tributary river of the Ganga. Originates in the Yamunotri glacier - merges with the Ganga river at Triveni Sangam at Prayagraj. Length:1,376 km.

• The **Brahmaputra river** - also called as Tsangpo. A trans-boundary river which flows through China, India, and Bangladesh. Important river in terms of irrigation, hydroelectricity generation, and transportation.

title: Environmental Pollution
text:
Environmental Pollution › Environmental Pollution › Environmental Pollution — Revision note (part 1/3)

• Pollution means the presence of an impurity or harmful pollutants in the environment.

**Types of pollution:**

**1. Air pollution-**
  • Air pollution is caused by hazardous gases and particles released from automobiles and industries. Also, caused by the smoke emitting from forest fires, gases emitted from decaying plant and animal materials, CFC(Chlorofluorocarbons) gases, etc.

• **Effects of air pollution:** Air pollution, if severe, leads to tuberculosis, breathing diseases, lung cancer, etc. in humans.
  - Plants are affected by low quality air.
  -The Greenhouse gases(GHGs) in the atmosphere leads to an increase in the temperature of the earth, which contributes to Global warming.

• **Control measures:-**
  a. Planting more trees.
  b. Using good quality petrol and diesel. Also, using clean fuels like CNG(Compressed Natural Gas).
  c. Installing Electrostatic precipitators(filtration devices) in the chimneys of the factories.
  d. Avoid the burning of crackers.
  e. Using clean energy obtained from solar cells, windmills, etc.
  f. Vehicular laws should be made more strict.

**2. Water pollution**-
  • Water pollution is causedby letting of untreated sewage from industries, household waste, food processing wastes, chemical fertilizers, and pesticides from agricultural fields into rivers, lakes, seas, etc.

• **Effects of water pollution:**Polluted water causes diseases like typhoid, hepatitis, cholera, chickenpox, dysentery, etc. in humans.
  -Water pollution disturbs the overall ecological balance of the water body and also harms aquatic animals.

**• Control measures:**Industrial waste or other domestic waste should be treated before discharging them into water bodies.
  -Drinking water should be properly treated to make it free from germs.

title: Environmental Pollution
text:
Environmental Pollution › Environmental Pollution › Environmental Pollution — Revision note (part 2/3)

**3. Soil pollution-
  • Soil pollution is caused**by chemical fertilizers, insecticides, pesticides that are used in agriculture.

**• Effects:**Agricultural runoff from the fields goes into the rivers; thus the fertilizers, pesticides, and insecticides get mixed with the river water and disturb the ecosystem there.

**• Control measures:**
  a. Minimum use of fertilizers, pesticides, insecticides should be done.
  b. The use of organic products in the farms should be encouraged.

**4. Noise pollution-
  • Caused**by excessive sound such as blaring loudspeakers, automobiles, industries, etc.

• **Effects:**Loss of hearing, loss of concentration, and lack of sleep in humans.

**• Control measures-**
 a. Noise barriers should be installed.
  b. More trees should be planted.

• **Waste-**
  • All the things that we use end up as waste.
  • Different types of waste:
  a. Solid waste, e.g., Car tyres, old books, furniture, etc.
  b. Liquid waste, e.g., Wastewater, chemical waste from industries, etc.
  c. Gaseous waste, e.g., Dust, smoke, etc.
  • Solid waste: biodegradable waste and non-biodegradable waste.

• **Biodegradable waste-**
  • Waste that can be broken down and decomposed into the soil by microorganisms.
  • It includes fruits, vegetable peels, leaves, wood, etc.

• **Non-biodegradable waste-**
  • Waste that cannot be broken down or decomposed into the soil.
  • It includes plastic, chemicals, polythene bags, etc.

• **Methods of waste disposal are:**

1. **Sanitary landfills**: Landfilling is mostly done outside the city in an open area, where the waste collected in dumpers and trucks is disposed off and spread over the land.

2.**Incineration(burning)**: It is the process wherein the waste is burnt at high temperatures. This produces a lot of smoke and carbon dioxide, which leads to air pollution. This is the easiest and quick way to dispose off the waste.

3. **Composting:** It is a natural process in which the organic material gets decomposed or transformed into a rich soil called compost. This compost, when added to the garden or household plants, benefits the plant growth.

• **Waste Management:**

India - 7th largest country in the world.

North-south extent of India - about 3200 km.

East-west extent - about 2900km.

[Figure 1]

**Physical Divisions of India -**

India is divided into 6 divisions - 1. The Himalayan Mountain ranges 2. The Northern Fertile Plains 3. The Great Indian Desert 4. The Southern Plateau region 5. The Coastal Plains and 6. Islands.

**1. The Himalayan Mountain ranges -**

• Covered by snow throughout the year.

• Extend from Jammu and Kashmir in the west to Arunachal Pradesh in the east.

• 2500km - length. Width varies from 150 to 400km.

• Mount Everest (8848m) - world's highest peak - located in the Himalayan mountain range.

• Other important peaks in the Himalayas are - Mt. K2 (8611m), Mt. Kangchenjunga (8598 m), Mt. Makalu (8462m), Mt. Dhaulagiri (8167m), Mt. Nandadevi (7817m).

The Himalayas consist of 3 parallel ranges -

a) The Himadri or the Great Himalayas -

• Northernmost range.

• Includes Mount Everest (8848m) - world's highest peak. Covered by snow throughout the year.

• Consists of glaciers which are a source of many rivers like - Ganga, Yamuna, Brahmaputra, Indus etc.

• Rivers get water due to melting of snow during summer season and rainwater during the rainy season.

b) The Himachal or the Lesser Himalayas -

• Lies to the south of the Himadri.

• Is lower in height as compared to the Great Himalayas or Himadri.

• Moderate elevation - so many hill stations are found here. E.g. Srinagar, Pahalgam, Gulmarg, Shimla, Manali, Nainital, Dalhousie, Darjeeling, etc.

• Covered with coniferous forests of pine, deodar, and chir trees.

• Terrace farming is practised on the mountain slopes.

c) The Shivaliks -

• Southernmost range of the Himalayas. Lies at the base of the Himalayas.

• Hill slopes of Shivaliks - covered with thick forests rich in wildlife.

• Animals found - tigers, crocodiles, leopards, bears, sambhar deers, etc. Bhabhar and the Terai belt - Lies between the Himalayas and the Northern Plains of India.

• Bhabhar - belt consisting of big and small rock pieces.

• Terai - belt consisting of swampy and marshy land.

**2. The Northern Plains -**

• Located to the south of Himalayan mountain ranges.

• Flat, level land extending from Punjab in the west to Assam in the east.

• Length of around 2400 km and breadth varying between 240 to 320 km.

• Formed by 3 major river systems- the Indus, the Ganga, and the Brahmaputra along with their tributaries.

The Northern Plains are subdivided as -

a) The Punjab Plains -

• Western part of the Northern plains formed by rivers Indus along with its tributaries, Jhelum, Chenab, Ravi, Beas and Satluj.

• Mostly lies in Pakistan and in India in the states of Punjab and Haryana.

• The Bhakra Nangal dam built on river Satluj is one of the largest dams in India.

• Agriculture is the main occupation. Wheat is the main crop grown here.

• Other important crops grown - rice, cotton, maize, sugarcane, barley and oilseeds.

b) The Ganga Plains -

• Also called - Gangetic Plains.

• Extends between river Ghaghar to River Teesta. It covers Haryana, Delhi, Uttar Pradesh, and West Bengal as well as some parts of Jharkhand.

• The major rivers flowing in this region - Ganga, Yamuna, Gandhak, Kosi, and Teesta.

• River Ganga originates from the Gangotri glacier.

• Rivers Bhagirathi - joined by rivers Alakhnanda and Mandakini. The combined flow of these tributaries forms the main river, Ganga.

• Agriculture is the main occupation.

• Main crops grown - wheat, rice, sugarcane, and jute.

• This region also called as the 'food bowl of India'.

• Important towns and cities situated on the banks of river Ganga, Yamuna and their tributaries -Haridwar, Rishikesh, Delhi, Agra, Kanpur, Allahabad (now known as Prayagraj), Varanasi, Patna, Kolkata, etc.

c) The Brahmaputra Basin -

• Lies in the state of Assam.

• River Brahmaputra originates in Tibet - called as river Tsangpo. Enters India through Arunachal Pradesh. Flows through Assam, Bangladesh and drains in the Bay of Bengal.

• One of the highest rainfall regions of the world.

• Main crops grown - rice and jute. Tea - on the hill slopes. Assam - well known for tea.

**3. The Peninsular Plateau or the Southern Plateau -**

• Triangular landmass lying to the south of Northern Plains.

• Extends from the south of Northern plains upto Kanyakumari. Called the Peninsular plateau or the Southern plateau. River Narmada forms a boundary which divides the Southern plateau into 2 parts.

a. Central Highlands - The part located to the north of river Narmada.

b. Deccan plateau The part located to the south of River Narmada.

Main plateaus -

a. The Malwa Plateau -

• Part of the Central Highlands - located to the north of river Narmada.

• Lies between the Aravalli range and the Vindhya range.

• Fertile black soil - suitable for cultivation of cotton.

b. The Chota Nagpur Plateau -

• Situated in the northeastern part of the Southern plateau.

• Extends in - Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, and Northern Odisha.

• Rich in mineral resources - coal, iron, manganese, and mica.

• Has large iron and steel plants - Jamshedpur and Bokaro (Jharkhand), and Rourkela (Odisha).

c. The Deccan Plateau -

• Uneven, rocky surface. Covers major parts of Maharashtra, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, and Telangana.
